arXiv:2108.09244v2 [math.CA] 19 May 2022

Convolution of beta prime distribution

Rui A. C. Ferreira Address: Grupo Física-Matemática, Faculdade de Ciências, Universidade de Lisboa, Av. Prof. Gama Pinto 2, 1649-003 Lisboa, Portugal. Email: raferreira@fc.ul.pt and Thomas Simon Address: Université de Lille, CNRS, UMR 8524 - Laboratoire Paul Painlevé, 59000 Lille, France. Email: thomas.simon@univ-lille.fr
Abstract.

We establish some identities in law for the convolution of a beta prime distribution with itself, involving the square root of beta distributions. The proof of these identities relies on transformations on generalized hypergeometric series obtained via Appell series of the first kind and Thomae’s relationships for F23​(1){}_{3}F_{2}(1). Using a self-decomposability argument, the identities are applied to derive complete monotonicity properties for quotients of confluent hypergeometric functions having a doubling character. By means of probability, we also obtain a simple proof of Turán’s inequality for the parabolic cylinder function and the confluent hypergeometric function of the second kind. The case of Mill’s ratio is discussed in detail.

Key words and phrases: 
Appell series; Beta prime distribution; Complete monotonicity; Confluent hypergeometric function; Hypergeometric series; Mill’s ratio; Parabolic cylinder function; Self-decomposability; Stochastic ordering; Thomae’s relations; Thorin measure; Turán’s inequality
2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
26A48; 33C15; 33C20; 33C45; 33C65; 60E07; 60E15; 62E15

1. Introduction

The beta prime random variable 𝐁a,b′{\bf B}^{\prime}_{a,b} with parameters a,b>0a,b>0 is a positive random variable with density

Γ⁡(a+b)Γ⁡(a)​Γ​(b)​xa−1(1+x)a+b\frac{{\Gamma}(a+b)}{{\Gamma}(a){\Gamma}(b)}\,\frac{x^{a-1}}{(1+x)^{a+b}}

on (0,∞).(0,\infty). This distribution is well-known in statistics as a generalization of the classical Fisher-Snedecor distribution: if d1,d2d_{1},d_{2} are positive integers and χ2​(d1),χ2​(d2)\chi_{2}(d_{1}),\chi_{2}(d_{2}) are two independent chi-squared random variables with respective parameters d1,d2d_{1},d_{2}, then the ratio

χ2​(d1)χ2​(d2)\frac{\chi_{2}(d_{1})}{\chi_{2}(d_{2})}

which is used in testing the equality of variances, is distributed as 𝐁d12,d22′.{\bf B}^{\prime}_{\frac{d_{1}}{2},\frac{d_{2}}{2}}. In general, one has the identities

𝐁a,b′=d1𝐁b,a− 1=d𝚪a𝚪b{\bf B}^{\prime}_{a,b}\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\;\frac{1}{{\bf B}_{b,a}}\,-\,1\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\;\frac{{\bf\Gamma}_{a}}{{\bf\Gamma}_{b}} (1)

where 𝐁p,q{\bf B}_{p,q} and 𝚪t{\bf\Gamma}_{t} denote for every p,q,t>0p,q,t>0 the standard beta and gamma random variables with respective densities

Γ⁡(p+q)Γ⁡(p)​Γ​(q)​xp−1​(1−x)q−1​ 1(0,1)​(x)and1Γ⁡(t)​xt−1​e−x​ 1(0,∞)​(x)\frac{{\Gamma}(p+q)}{{\Gamma}(p){\Gamma}(q)}\,x^{p-1}(1-x)^{q-1}\,{\bf 1}_{(0,1)}(x)\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad\frac{1}{{\Gamma}(t)}\,x^{t-1}e^{-x}\,{\bf 1}_{(0,\infty)}(x)

and, here and throughout, all random variables appearing on one side of an identity in law are assumed to be independent unless otherwise explicitly stated. In the statistical literature, the beta prime distribution is sometimes called the beta distribution of the second kind, the generalized F−F-distribution or the Pearson type VI distribution, and we refer to Chapter 27 in [3] for an account.

The Mellin transform of the beta prime distribution is given as

𝔼⁡[(𝐁a,b′)s]=Γ⁡(a+s)​Γ​(b−s)Γ⁡(a)​Γ​(b){\mathbb{E}}[({\bf B}^{\prime}_{a,b})^{s}]\;=\;\frac{{\Gamma}(a+s){\Gamma}(b-s)}{{\Gamma}(a){\Gamma}(b)} (2)

for every s∈(−a,b),s\in(-a,b), whereas its Laplace transform reads

𝔼⁡[e−z​𝐁a,b′]=Γ⁡(a+b)Γ⁡(a)​Γ​(b)​∫0∞e−z​t​ta−1​(1+t)−a−b​𝑑t=Γ⁡(a+b)Γ⁡(b)​Ψ​(a,1−b,z){\mathbb{E}}[e^{-z{\bf B}^{\prime}_{a,b}}]\;=\;\frac{{\Gamma}(a+b)}{{\Gamma}(a){\Gamma}(b)}\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-zt}t^{a-1}(1+t)^{-a-b}\,dt\;=\;\frac{{\Gamma}(a+b)}{{\Gamma}(b)}\,\Psi(a,1-b,z) (3)

for every z≥0z\geq 0, where Ψ\Psi is the confluent hypergeometric function of the second kind - see Formula 6.5.(2) in [11]. This connection with the Ψ\Psi function was used by Ismail and Kelker in [14] to show, by Stieltjes inversion, the non-obvious fact that the beta prime distribution is self-decomposable (SD), in other words that for every a,b>0a,b>0 and λ∈(0,1),\lambda\in(0,1), there is a decomposition

𝐁a,b′=dλ​𝐁a,b′+𝐗a,b,λ{\bf B}^{\prime}_{a,b}\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\;\lambda\,{\bf B}^{\prime}_{a,b}\;+\;{\bf X}_{a,b,\lambda}

for some positive, infinitely divisible (ID) random variable 𝐗a,b,λ.{\bf X}_{a,b,\lambda}. This property is characterized by the following Lévy-Khintchine representation of Ψ⁡(a,c,z)\Psi(a,c,z) which is a consequence of (1.4) in [14] by integration:

Ψ⁡(a,c,z)=Γ⁡(1−c)Γ⁡(a+1−c)​exp−(∫0∞(1−e−z​t)​t−1​ka,c​(t)​𝑑t)\Psi(a,c,z)\;=\;\frac{{\Gamma}(1-c)}{{\Gamma}(a+1-c)}\,\exp\,-\left(\int_{0}^{\infty}(1-e^{-zt})\,t^{-1}\,k_{a,c}(t)\,dt\right)

for every a,z>0a,z>0 and c<1,c<1, with

ka,c​(t)=∫0∞e−t​y​(y−c​e−y​|Ψ⁡(a,c,y​ei​π)|−2Γ⁡(a)​Γ​(a+1−c))​𝑑yk_{a,c}(t)\;=\;\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-ty}\left(\frac{y^{-c}e^{-y}\left|\Psi(a,c,ye^{{\rm i}\pi})\right|^{-2}}{{\Gamma}(a){\Gamma}(a+1-c)}\right)dy

a decreasing function on (0,∞).(0,\infty). In probabilistic terms, this formula means that the Lévy measure of the self-decomposable random variable 𝐁a,b′{\bf B}^{\prime}_{a,b} is expressed in terms of the values on the cut of the same confluent hypergeometric function Ψ⁡(a,1−b,z).\Psi(a,1-b,z). We refer e.g. to [8] p.18 for a brief, enough for our purposes in the present paper, account on self-decomposability. Throughout, we will use the classical fact that this class of distributions is closed w.r.t. convolution and weak convergence.

The Lévy-Khintchine representation means that Ψ⁡(a,c,z)\Psi(a,c,z) is for a>0a>0 and c<1c<1 not only completely monotone (CM) as the renormalized Laplace transform of a beta prime random variable, but also logarithmically completely monotone (LCM), that is the logarithmic derivative z↦−(log⁡Ψ⁡(a,c,z))′z\mapsto-(\log\Psi(a,c,z))^{\prime} is CM. Throughout the paper, the CM property will be implicitly meant on (0,∞).(0,\infty). The completely monotonic character of the spectral function ka,ck_{a,c} itself means a stronger property for the beta prime distribution which is called the generalized gamma convolution and amounts to the stochastic integral representation

𝐁a,b′=d∫0aλa,b​(t)​d​γt,{\bf B}^{\prime}_{a,b}\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\;\int_{0}^{a}\!\lambda_{a,b}(t)\,d\gamma_{t},

where {γt,t≥0}\{\gamma_{t},\;t\geq 0\} is the standard Gamma subordinator and {λa,b​(t),t∈[0,a]}\{\lambda_{a,b}(t),\;t\in[0,a]\} some deterministic function that can be recovered from ka,1−b.k_{a,1-b}. Notice that the upper integration bound a=ka,1−b​(0)a=k_{a,1-b}(0) corresponds to the power law behaviour in xa−1x^{a-1} at zero for the density of 𝐁a,b′.{\bf B}^{\prime}_{a,b}. In this respect, the function t↦a−1​ka,1−b​(t)t\mapsto a^{-1}k_{a,1-b}(t) is the Laplace transform of a positive random variable 𝐆a,b{\bf G}_{a,b} which is called the Thorin random variable associated to 𝐁a,b′{\bf B}^{\prime}_{a,b}. The distribution of 𝐆a,b{\bf G}_{a,b} is quite interesting and will be reviewed in Section 2. We refer to chapters 3 and 4 in [8] and Section 1 in [16] for accounts on generalized Gamma convolutions and Thorin random variables, including the proofs of the above facts. We also mention that around the same time when [14] was written, it was observed by Bondesson and Thorin that the density of 𝐁a,b′{\bf B}^{\prime}_{a,b} is the prototype of a so-called hyperbolically completely monotone (HCM) density, which has stronger properties than the densities of generalized Gamma convolutions. We refer to Chapter 5 in [8] for more information on this notion, which we will briefly use in Section 5.

In this paper, we investigate the structure of the addition of two independent beta prime random variables. This problem, which is naturally connected to the semigroup property underlying the random variable 𝐁a,b′{\bf B}^{\prime}_{a,b}, was investigated in [10] with motivations coming from Bayesian analysis and multivariate testing. In particular, a general and rather complicated formula for the distribution function is given in [10] in terms of some Lauricella function in three variables, which was later simplified in [12] into an Appell series in two variables. Our main purpose here is to display some simple, albeit non-trivial, identities in law having a rather surprising character involving a product, a sum and a square root. Our first result is the following.

Theorem A​​ .

For every a>0,a>0, one has

𝐁a,1/2′+𝐁a,1/2′=d𝐁2​a,1/2′×(1+𝐁a,1/2).{\bf B}^{\prime}_{a,1/2}\,+\,{\bf B}^{\prime}_{a,1/2}\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\;{\bf B}^{\prime}_{2a,1/2}\,\times\left(1\,+\,\sqrt{{\bf B}_{a,1/2}}\right).

This identity, which should be compared with the well-known identities

1𝚪1/2+1𝚪1/2=d4𝚪1/2and𝚪a+𝚪a=d𝚪2​a,\frac{1}{{\bf\Gamma}_{1/2}}\;+\;\frac{1}{{\bf\Gamma}_{1/2}}\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\;\frac{4}{{\bf\Gamma}_{1/2}}\qquad\quad\mbox{and}\qquad\quad{\bf\Gamma}_{a}\;+\;{\bf\Gamma}_{a}\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\;{\bf\Gamma}_{2a},

amounts to the computation of the law of a certain “Dirichlet mean” associated to the Thorin random variable 𝐆a,1/2:{\bf G}_{a,1/2}: with the notation of [16], to which we refer for details on Dirichlet means, one has

Da(𝐆a,1/2)=d1𝚪1/2andD2​a(𝐆a,1/2)=d1+𝐁a,1/2𝚪1/2⋅D_{a}({\bf G}_{a,1/2})\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\;\frac{1}{{\bf\Gamma}_{1/2}}\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad D_{2a}({\bf G}_{a,1/2})\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\;\frac{1+\sqrt{{\bf B}_{a,1/2}}}{{\bf\Gamma}_{1/2}}\cdot

Apart from its exactitude, our motivation for the above result comes from sharp bounds, monotonicity and complete monotonicity properties for quotients of confluent hypergeometric functions. The complete monotonicity of the ratio

Ψ⁡(a+1,c+1,z)Ψ⁡(a,c,z)\frac{\Psi(a+1,c+1,z)}{\Psi(a,c,z)}

for every a>0a>0 and c<1,c<1, which is equivalent to the infinite divisibility of 𝐁a,b′{\bf B}^{\prime}_{a,b} for every a,b>0,a,b>0, was established in [14] and has influenced ever since a substantial body of works devoted to such questions for quotients of various classes of special functions. We refer to [5, 6, 15, 18, 20, 23, 25, 26, 28, 30] for a few examples of this literature, which is still ongoing. The approach which is generally followed in these papers is analytical and often relies on the second order ODE associated to the class of special functions in consideration. As in the aforementioned result of [14], this leads to a discrete difference between the parameters of the two special functions appearing in the quotient. This discrete gap is also observed in the so-called Turán inequalities, an emblematic example of which is the recently established - see [18] - monotonicity on ℝ{\mathbb{R}} of the quotient of parabolic cylinder functions

(D−ν−1​(z))2D−ν​(z)​D−ν−2​(z)\frac{(D_{-\nu-1}(z))^{2}}{D_{-\nu}(z)D_{-\nu-2}(z)}

for every ν>0.\nu>0. In the present paper, we take a probabilistic point of view and show properties of this kind with a difference in the parameters which is continous. Typical results that we obtain are the complete monotonocity of

Ψ⁡(a,c,z)Ψ⁡(a,c′,z)\frac{\Psi(a,c,z)}{\Psi(a,c^{\prime},z)}

for every a>0a>0 and c′<c<1c^{\prime}<c<1 which is proved by self-decomposability - see Corollary 1, and the monotonicity on ℝ{\mathbb{R}} of

(D−ν−c​(z))2D−ν​(z)​D−ν−2​c​(z)\frac{(D_{-\nu-c}(z))^{2}}{D_{-\nu}(z)D_{-\nu-2c}(z)}

for every ν,c>0,\nu,c>0, which we derive through the connection with generalized half-Gaussian distributions - see Proposition 9. The self-decomposability argument also implies as a by-product of Theorem A the complete monotonicity of the quotient of Hermite function

(H−ν​(z))2H−2​ν​(z)\frac{(H_{-\nu}(\sqrt{z}))^{2}}{H_{-2\nu}(\sqrt{z})}

for every ν>0,\nu>0, whose “doubling character” is less usual than the previous results. For ν∈(0,2]\nu\in(0,2], a stochastic comparison of the distribution of the Dirichlet means Da​(𝐆a,1/2)D_{a}({\bf G}_{a,1/2}) and D2​a​(𝐆a,1/2),D_{2a}({\bf G}_{a,1/2}), and a general formula due to [16] imply that the above quotient is actually LCM, in other words that its associated random variable is compound Poisson - see Corollary 4. In the last part of this paper, these results allow us to derive a series of properties of the classical Mill’s ratio, including a new proof of Sampford’s inequality.

Our second exact result for the convolution of a beta prime distribution is the following identity.

Theorem B​​ .

For every b∈(0,1/2),b\in(0,1/2), one has

𝐁a,b′+𝐁a,b′=d𝐁2​a,b′×(1+𝐁a,1/2𝐁b,1/2−b){\bf B}^{\prime}_{a,b}\,+\,{\bf B}^{\prime}_{a,b}\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\;{\bf B}^{\prime}_{2a,b}\,\times\left(1\,+\,\sqrt{\frac{{\bf B}_{a,1/2}}{{\bf B}_{b,1/2-b}}}\right)

if a=1−ba=1-b or a=1/2.a=1/2.

In the case a=1/2,a=1/2, this result recovers Theorem A in letting b→1/2b\to 1/2 and 𝐁b,1/2−b⟶d1.{\bf B}_{b,1/2-b}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\longrightarrow}}1. The appearance of a third random variable on the right-hand side of the identity makes Theorem B significantly harder to prove than Theorem A. Whereas the latter relies on rather classical considerations on the hypergeometric series F12​(z),{}_{2}F_{1}(z), the analysis underlying the proof of the former makes an extensive use of the generalized series F23​(z),{}_{3}F_{2}(z), where the corresponding formulæ  are more sparse. Our argument is based on certain transformations of the Mellin transform of the left-hand side, where Thomae’s relationships on F23​(1){}_{3}F_{2}(1) play their role, and the comparison of certain densities obtained via some non-trivial reduction formulæ  on Appell series of the first kind. A key-argument is also the transformation of a certain F23​(1){}_{3}F_{2}(1) into some F23​(−1),{}_{3}F_{2}(-1), which is necessary to obtain a random variable of the type 𝐁2​a,b′×(1+𝐗){\bf B}^{\prime}_{2a,b}\times(1+{\bf X}) on the right-hand side. Unfortunately, this transformation is possible only in certain specific situations and this explains our limitation on the range of the parameters. As a further, negative, result, we prove by stochastic ordering that for every a>0,a>0, an identity in law with a random variable of the type 𝐁2​a,b′×(1+𝐗){\bf B}^{\prime}_{2a,b}\times(1+{\bf X}) on the right-hand side cannot hold if b>1b>1 - see Proposition 7. On the other hand, we do believe that the statement of Theorem B is valid for every a>0a>0 and b∈(0,1/2)b\in(0,1/2) and it is our hope that this probabilistic problem, which is equivalent to a non-conventional integral representation for a family of F23​(1){}_{3}F_{2}(1)’s, can stimulate readers having a deeper grip on generalized hypergeometric series.

2. Preliminaries

In this section, we exploit an elementary identity in law stated as Proposition 1, in order to derive a CM property for quotients of Ψ\Psi functions by a self-decomposability argument. The same argument will be used in the next section to deduce some further CM properties from the more involved Theorems A and B. In the case a≤1,a\leq 1, we also obtain a closed and non-trivial formula for the cumulative Thorin measure of 𝐁a,b′{\bf B}^{\prime}_{a,b} which is used to derive the stronger LCM property. In passing, we establish a connection between this Thorin measure and the so-called Askey-Wimp-Kerov distribution.

Proposition 1.

For every b′>b>0b^{\prime}>b>0 and a>0,a>0, one has

𝐁a,b′=d𝐁a,b′′×(1+𝐁b′−b,b′){\bf B}^{\prime}_{a,b}\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\;{\bf B}^{\prime}_{a,b^{\prime}}\,\times\left(1\,+\,{\bf B}^{\prime}_{b^{\prime}\!-b,b}\right)
Proof.

The factorization

𝚪b=d𝚪b′×𝐁b,b′−b{\bf\Gamma}_{b}\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\;{\bf\Gamma}_{b^{\prime}}\,\times\,{\bf B}_{b,b^{\prime}\!-b} (4)

is well-known and follows from the computation of the Mellin transform on both sides. Plugging this into (1) implies

𝐁a,b′=d𝐁a,b′′×𝐁b,b′−b−1=d𝐁a,b′′×(1+𝐁b′−b,b′){\bf B}^{\prime}_{a,b}\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\;{\bf B}^{\prime}_{a,b^{\prime}}\,\times\,{\bf B}_{b,b^{\prime}\!-b}^{-1}\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\;{\bf B}^{\prime}_{a,b^{\prime}}\,\times\left(1\,+\,{\bf B}^{\prime}_{b^{\prime}\!-b,b}\right)

as required. □\square

As a consequence of this identity in law, we obtain our first complete monotonicity property.

Corollary 1.

For every a>0a>0 and c′<c<1,c^{\prime}<c<1, the function

z↦Ψ⁡(a,c,z)Ψ⁡(a,c′,z)z\;\mapsto\;\frac{\Psi(a,c,z)}{\Psi(a,c^{\prime},z)}

is CM.

Proof.

Set b=1−c,b′=1−c′b=1-c,b^{\prime}=1-c^{\prime} with b′>b>0.b^{\prime}>b>0. As discussed in the introduction, the random variable 𝐁a,b′′{\bf B}^{\prime}_{a,b^{\prime}} is SD, and this implies that conditionally on 𝐁b′−b,b′=x≥0,{\bf B}^{\prime}_{b^{\prime}\!-b,b}=x\geq 0, the law of the independent product 𝐁a,b′′×(1+𝐁b′−b,b′)=(1+x)​𝐁a,b′′{\bf B}^{\prime}_{a,b^{\prime}}\,\times(1\,+\,{\bf B}^{\prime}_{b^{\prime}\!-b,b})=(1+x)\,{\bf B}^{\prime}_{a,b^{\prime}} is that of the independent sum

𝐁a,b′′+𝐗xa,b′{\bf B}^{\prime}_{a,b^{\prime}}\,+\,{\bf X}^{a,b^{\prime}}_{x}

for some non-negative random variable 𝐗xa,b′.{\bf X}^{a,b^{\prime}}_{x}\!\!. Integrating shows, by Proposition 1, the additive factorization

𝐁a,b′=d𝐁a,b′′+𝐘a,b,b′{\bf B}^{\prime}_{a,b}\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\;{\bf B}^{\prime}_{a,b^{\prime}}\;+\;{\bf Y}_{a,b,b^{\prime}}

with the notation 𝐗𝐁b′−b,b′a,b′=𝐘a,b,b′≥0.{\bf X}^{a,b^{\prime}}_{{\bf B}^{\prime}_{b^{\prime}\!-b,b}}\!\!\!={\bf Y}_{a,b,b^{\prime}}\geq 0. By (3), we deduce the representation

Ψ⁡(a,c,z)Ψ⁡(a,c′,z)=Γ⁡(a+b)​Γ​(b′)Γ⁡(a+b′)​Γ​(b)​𝔼​[e−z​𝐘a,b,b′],\frac{\Psi(a,c,z)}{\Psi(a,c^{\prime},z)}\;=\;\frac{{\Gamma}(a+b){\Gamma}(b^{\prime})}{{\Gamma}(a+b^{\prime}){\Gamma}(b)}\;{\mathbb{E}}\left[e^{-z{\bf Y}_{a,b,b^{\prime}}}\right],

which concludes the proof by Bernstein’s theorem.

□\square

Remark 1.

For every a>0a>0 and 1<c<c′<1+a,1<c<c^{\prime}<1+a, Kummer’s transformation - see Formula 6.5.(6) in [11] - implies that

z↦zc−c′​Ψ⁡(a+c−c′,c,z)Ψ⁡(a,c′,z)=Ψ⁡(1+a−c′,2−c,z)Ψ⁡(1+a−c′,2−c′,z)z\;\mapsto\;z^{c-c^{\prime}}\,\frac{\Psi(a+c-c^{\prime},c,z)}{\Psi(a,c^{\prime},z)}\;=\;\frac{\Psi(1+a-c^{\prime},2-c,z)}{\Psi(1+a-c^{\prime},2-c^{\prime},z)}

is also CM. The complete monotonicity of

z↦Ψ⁡(a+c−c′,c,z)Ψ⁡(a,c′,z)z\;\mapsto\;\frac{\Psi(a+c-c^{\prime},c,z)}{\Psi(a,c^{\prime},z)}

for every a>0a>0 and c′<c<1c^{\prime}<c<1 is conjectured in Problem 7.2 in [14] and we will come back to this question in Remark 2 (d) below.

We next obtain the following reinforcement of Corollary 1 in the case a≤1.a\leq 1. The argument relies on an appropriate expression for the cumulative Thorin measure of the beta prime distribution.

Corollary 2.

For every a∈(0,1]a\in(0,1] and c′<c<1,c^{\prime}<c<1, the function

z↦Ψ⁡(a,c,z)Ψ⁡(a,c′,z)z\;\mapsto\;\frac{\Psi(a,c,z)}{\Psi(a,c^{\prime},z)}

is LCM.

Proof.

Taking the pointwise limit, it is enough to consider the case a∈(0,1).a\in(0,1). The LCM property amounts to the ID property of the above random variable 𝐘a,b,b′,{\bf Y}_{a,b,b^{\prime}}, where we have again set b=1−cb=1-c and b′=1−c′.b^{\prime}=1-c^{\prime}. Recall from the self-decomposability of 𝐁a,b′′{\bf B}^{\prime}_{a,b^{\prime}} that the random variable 𝐗xa,b′{\bf X}^{a,b^{\prime}}_{x} in the above proof is ID for every x>0.x>0. On the other hand, the ID property may not be preserved by mixtures. From the above decomposition, we see that the log-Laplace transform of 𝐘a,b,b′{\bf Y}_{a,b,b^{\prime}} is given by

−log⁡𝔼⁡[e−z​𝐘a,b,b′]=∫0∞(1−e−z​y)​(μa,b−μa,b′)​(𝑑y)-\log{\mathbb{E}}\left[e^{-z{\bf Y}_{a,b,b^{\prime}}}\right]\;=\;\int_{0}^{\infty}(1-e^{-zy})(\mu_{a,b}-\mu_{a,b^{\prime}})(dy) (5)

where μa,x\mu_{a,x} is the Lévy measure of 𝐁a,x′{\bf B}^{\prime}_{a,x} for x=b,b′.x=b,b^{\prime}. The density of μa,x\mu_{a,x} on (0,∞)(0,\infty) can be recovered from (1.4) of [14], which implies from (3) and the Lévy-Khintchine formula that (here and throughout, Ψz′\Psi^{\prime}_{z} denotes the derivative of Ψ\Psi w.r.t. to zz)

∫0∞y​e−z​y​μa,x​(𝑑y)=−Ψz′​(a,1−x,z)Ψ⁡(a,1−x,z)=a​Ψ​(a+1,2−x,z)Ψ⁡(a,1−x,z)=a​∫0∞e−z​y​𝔼​[e−y​𝐆a,x]​𝑑y\int_{0}^{\infty}y\,e^{-zy}\,\mu_{a,x}(dy)\;=\;-\frac{\Psi^{\prime}_{z}(a,1-x,z)}{\Psi(a,1-x,z)}\;=\;\frac{a\Psi(a+1,2-x,z)}{\Psi(a,1-x,z)}\;=\;a\int_{0}^{\infty}\!\!e^{-zy}\,{\mathbb{E}}[e^{-y{\bf G}_{a,x}}]\,dy

where 𝐆a,x{\bf G}_{a,x} is a positive random variable with density

3. Proof of Theorem A

We begin with a general formula for the density of λ​𝐁a,b′+μ​𝐁c,d′\lambda{\bf B}^{\prime}_{a,b}+\mu{\bf B}^{\prime}_{c,d} in terms of the first Appell series F1F_{1}, which is more convenient for our purposes than the ones previously obtained in [10, 12] for the distribution function. This formula will also be used later on in Section 5. We refer to [1] and to sections 5.7-14 in [11] for classic accounts on Appell series.

Proposition 2.

For every a,b,c,d,λ,μ>0,a,b,c,d,\lambda,\mu>0, the density of λ​𝐁a,b′+μ​𝐁c,d′\lambda{\bf B}^{\prime}_{a,b}+\mu{\bf B}^{\prime}_{c,d} reads

Γ⁡(c+d)​λ−a​μd​xa+c−1Γ⁡(c)​Γ​(d)​(x+μ)c+dF1(a,a+b,c+d,a+c;−x/λ,x/(x+μ))\frac{{\Gamma}(c+d)\lambda^{-a}\mu^{d}\,x^{a+c-1}}{{\Gamma}(c){\Gamma}(d)\,(x+\mu)^{c+d}}\,F_{1}\left(a,a+b,c+d,a+c;-x/\lambda,x/(x+\mu)\right)

on (0,∞).(0,\infty).

Proof.

The convolution formula and a change of variable show first that the density of λ​𝐁a,b′+μ​𝐁c,d′\lambda{\bf B}^{\prime}_{a,b}+\mu{\bf B}^{\prime}_{c,d} is

Γ⁡(a+b)​Γ​(c+d)​λb​μd​xa+c−1Γ⁡(a)​Γ​(b)​Γ​(c)​Γ​(d)​∫01ya−1​(1−y)c−1(λ+x​y)a+b​(x+μ−x​y)c+d​𝑑y.\frac{{\Gamma}(a+b){\Gamma}(c+d)\lambda^{b}\mu^{d}\,x^{a+c-1}}{{\Gamma}(a){\Gamma}(b){\Gamma}(c){\Gamma}(d)}\,\int_{0}^{1}\!\frac{y^{a-1}(1-y)^{c-1}}{(\lambda+xy)^{a+b}\,(x+\mu-xy)^{c+d}}\,dy. (10)

By Picard’s integral formula - see Formulæ  5.7.(6) and 5.8.2.(5) in [11], we obtain the required expression as an Appell series of the first kind.

□\square

We next give a simpler expression in terms of the hypergeometric function for the density of 𝐁a,b′+𝐁a,b′{\bf B}^{\prime}_{a,b}+{\bf B}^{\prime}_{a,b} which we will, throughout, denote by φa,b.{\varphi_{a,b}}. This expression will be our starting point for the hypergeometric identities which will be used henceforth.

on (0,∞).(0,\infty).

Proof.

Letting λ=μ=1\lambda=\mu=1 and (a,b)=(c,d)(a,b)=(c,d) in (10), the integral transforms into

2​Γ​(a+b)2​x2​a−1Γ​(a)2​Γ​(b)2​∫01/2(y⁡(1−y))a−1(x+1+x2​y​(1−y))a+b​𝑑y\frac{2\,{\Gamma}(a+b)^{2}\,x^{2a-1}}{{\Gamma}(a)^{2}{\Gamma}(b)^{2}}\,\int_{0}^{1/2}\!\frac{(y(1-y))^{a-1}}{(x+1+x^{2}y(1-y))^{a+b}}\,dy

and then, making the substitution z=4​y​(1−y),z=4y(1-y), into

21−2​a​Γ​(a+b)2​x2​a−1Γ​(a)2​Γ​(b)2​(x+1)a+b​∫01za−1(1−z)−1/2(1+x2​z/4​(x+1))a+b​𝑑z.\frac{2^{1-2a}\,{\Gamma}(a+b)^{2}\,x^{2a-1}}{{\Gamma}(a)^{2}{\Gamma}(b)^{2}\,(x+1)^{a+b}}\,\int_{0}^{1}\!\frac{z^{a-1}(1-z)^{-1/2}}{(1+x^{2}z/4(x+1))^{a+b}}\,dz.

In the case c∈(1/2,1),c\in(1/2,1), this would be a consequence of the following extension of Theorem B.

Conjecture 1.

For every a>0a>0 and b∈(0,1/2),b\in(0,1/2), one has

𝐁a,b′+𝐁a,b′=d𝐁2​a,b′×(1+𝐁a,1/2𝐁b,1/2−b).{\bf B}^{\prime}_{a,b}\,+\,{\bf B}^{\prime}_{a,b}\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\;{\bf B}^{\prime}_{2a,b}\,\times\left(1\,+\,\sqrt{\frac{{\bf B}_{a,1/2}}{{\bf B}_{b,1/2-b}}}\right).

for every a>0,b∈(0,1/2)a>0,b\in(0,1/2) and s∈(−2​a,b).s\in(-2a,b). The non-conventional character of this representation comes from the square root inside the integral. In the cases a=1/2a=1/2 and a=1−b,a=1-b, we were able to show the representation essentially with the help of Thomae’s relations on F23​(1){}_{3}F_{2}(1) and the reduction of Appell series of the first kind, our main tools in the above proof. Unfortunately, we do not know as yet how to extend such arguments to the general case. There is a huge list of classic transformations on F23​(z){}_{3}F_{2}(z) displayed in Section 7.4. of [9], and in the case a=1/2a=1/2 we have made a crucial use of Formula 7.4.1.11. therein. Our feeling is that these classic transformations might not be enough to tackle Conjecture 1 in general. In this respect, let us refer to [19] for a recent and non-classical transformation on some F23​(1),{}_{3}F_{2}(1), which however does not seem to be very helpful for our problem. See also Remark 7 below for another integral representation of some F12​(z){}_{2}F_{1}(z) which would give an answer to Conjecture 1 in the case a+b=1/2.a+b=1/2.

5. Miscellaneous

5.1. The case a+b=1/2a+b=1/2

Remark 7.

It is natural to ask if Proposition 6 implies Conjecture 1. It is clear from (1) and (4) that this implication amounts to the identity

𝐁a,1/2+𝐁b,1/2−1=d𝐁b,b−1×(1+𝐁a,1/2𝐁b,a){\bf B}_{a,1/2}\,+\,{\bf B}_{b,1/2}^{-1}\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\;{\bf B}_{b,b}^{-1}\,\times\,\left(1\,+\,\sqrt{\frac{{\bf B}_{a,1/2}}{{\bf B}_{b,a}}}\right)

for a+b=1/2.a+b=1/2. It can be shown that the density of the r.v. on the left-hand side equals

on (1,2)∪(2,∞)(1,2)\cup(2,\infty) and is remarkably given by the same function on both intervals - a function which diverges at 2. The density of the r.v. on the right-hand side is a priori more complicated and equals

on (1,2).(1,2). In particular, the two densities have the same asymptotics as x↓1x\downarrow 1 and x↑2,x\uparrow 2, respectively given by

Γ⁡(b+1/2)​(x−1)a−1/2π​Γ​(b)andΓ⁡(a+1/2)​Γ​(b+1/2)π​Γ​(a)​Γ​(b)​log⁡(12−x).\frac{{\Gamma}(b+1/2)\,(x-1)^{a-1/2}}{\sqrt{\pi}\,{\Gamma}(b)}\qquad\quad\mbox{and}\quad\qquad\frac{{\Gamma}(a+1/2)\,{\Gamma}(b+1/2)}{\pi\,{\Gamma}(a)\,{\Gamma}(b)}\,\log\left(\frac{1}{2-x}\right).

5.3. Monotonicity properties

In this paragraph we establish a monotonicity property for the ratio of Ψ\Psi functions appearing in Conjecture 1, and we state a related open problem. We also give a simple proof of the Turán inequality for the Ψ\Psi function and the parabolic cylinder function recently obtained in [5, 18], together with a fractional extension. All these results rely on the following consequence of a classical lemma by Biernaki and Krzyż [7], which might be well-known but we could not find any reference.

Lemma 3.

Let f,gf,g be probability densities defined on an interval (a,b)⊆(0,∞)(a,b)\subseteq(0,\infty) which are positive, continuous, and such that the ratio x↦f⁡(x)/g⁡(x)x\mapsto f(x)/g(x) is non-decreasing on (a,b).(a,b). Then, the ratios

z↦∫0∞e−z​x​f​(x)​𝑑x∫0∞e−z​x​g​(x)​𝑑xandz↦∫0∞f⁡(x)(1+x​z)μ​𝑑x∫0∞g⁡(x)(1+x​z)μ​𝑑xz\;\mapsto\;\frac{{\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\!\!e^{-zx}f(x)\,dx}}{{\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\!\!e^{-zx}g(x)\,dx}}\qquad\quad\mbox{and}\qquad\quad z\;\mapsto\;\frac{{\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\!\!\frac{f(x)}{(1+xz)^{\mu}}\,dx}}{{\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\!\!\frac{g(x)}{(1+xz)^{\mu}}\,dx}}

are non-increasing on (0,∞)(0,\infty) for every μ>0.\mu>0.

Proof.

We start with the ratio of Laplace transforms. Suppose first b<∞b<\infty and fix some n∈ℕ∗.n\in{\mathbb{N}}^{*}. Consider the variate u=e−z(b−a)/nu=e^{-z(b-a)/n} and, for every i=1,…,n,i=1,\ldots,n, set xi=a+i⁡(b−a)/n,ai=f⁡(xi)x_{i}=a+i(b-a)/n,a_{i}=f(x_{i}) and bi=g⁡(xi).b_{i}=g(x_{i}). Since the sequence {ai/bi}\{a_{i}/b_{i}\} is non-decreasing, it follows from Biernaki and Krzyż’s lemma that the function

u↦∑i=1nai​ui∑i=1nbi​uiu\;\mapsto\;\frac{{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}u^{i}}}{{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}u^{i}}}

is non-decreasing on (0,1),(0,1), so that the function

z↦∑i=1ne−z​xi​f​(xi)∑i=1ne−z​xi​g​(xi)z\;\mapsto\;\frac{{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}e^{-zx_{i}}f(x_{i})}}{{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}e^{-zx_{i}}g(x_{i})}}

is non-increasing on (0,∞).(0,\infty). We can then conclude by taking the pointwise limit of the Riemann sums as n→∞.n\to\infty. The case b=∞b=\infty is analogous and we omit details. To handle the ratio of generalized Stieltjes transforms, it suffices to observe by a change of variable that

∫0∞f⁡(x)(1+x​z)μ​𝑑x∫0∞g⁡(x)(1+x​z)μ​𝑑x=∫0∞e−z−1​u​(uμ−1​∫0∞f⁡(x)​e−x​u​𝑑x)​𝑑u∫0∞e−z−1​u​(uμ−1​∫0∞g⁡(x)​e−x​u​𝑑x)​𝑑u⋅\frac{{\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\!\!\frac{f(x)}{(1+xz)^{\mu}}\,dx}}{{\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\!\!\frac{g(x)}{(1+xz)^{\mu}}\,dx}}\;=\;\frac{{\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\!\!e^{-z^{-1}u}\left(u^{\mu-1}\int_{0}^{\infty}f(x)\,e^{-xu}dx\right)du}}{{\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\!\!e^{-z^{-1}u}\left(u^{\mu-1}\int_{0}^{\infty}g(x)\,e^{-xu}dx\right)du}}\cdot

Hence, the monotonicity of the left-hand side can be deduced from that of the ratios of Laplace transforms. More precisely, the ratios of functions between brackets inside the integrals on the right-hand side is non-increasing in uu, so that the ratio on the left-hand side is non-decreasing in z−1z^{-1} and non-increasing in zz.

□\square

Remark 8.

For the ratio of Laplace transforms, it is easy to check that the monotonicity property extends on (c,∞)(c,\infty) with c∈[−∞,0)c\in[-\infty,0), provided both Laplace transforms are finite on (c,∞)(c,\infty).

Corollary 8.

For every a>0a>0 and c∈[1/2,1],c\in[1/2,1], the function

decreases on (0,∞).(0,\infty).

Proof.

Set b=1−c∈[0,1/2]b=1-c\in[0,1/2] and suppose first b>0.b>0. Using (3) and the notation of the proof of Proposition 7, we have

Ψ2​(a,c,z)Ψ⁡(2​a,c,z)=Γ⁡(b)​Γ​(2​a+b)(Γ⁡(a+b))2×(∫0∞e−z​x​φa,b​(x)​𝑑x∫0∞e−z​x​φ~a,b​(x)​𝑑x).\frac{\Psi^{2}(a,c,z)}{\Psi(2a,c,z)}\;=\;\frac{{\Gamma}(b){\Gamma}(2a+b)}{({\Gamma}(a+b))^{2}}\,\times\left(\frac{{\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\!\!e^{-zx}{\varphi_{a,b}}(x)\,dx}}{{\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\!\!e^{-zx}{{\widetilde{\varphi}}_{a,b}}(x)\,dx}}\right).

We have seen during the proof of Proposition 7 that the function

is non-increasing on (0,∞)(0,\infty) for every a>0a>0 and b∈(0,1/2],b\in(0,1/2], so that we can conclude by Lemma 3 that

In view of Corollaries 7 and 8, it is natural to state the following open problem, which might be challenging. Recall that in the case c∈[1/2,1]c\in[1/2,1] the open if part of this statement is, by self-decomposability, a consequence of Conjecture 1.

is CM if and only if c∈[0,1].c\in[0,1].

We refer to [6, 28] for some other, non-fractional, refinements of the Turán inequalities obtained in [5]. See in particular Corollaire 2 in [28] and Theorem 1 in [6] for different improvements of Theorem 2 in [5].

The random variable

Remark 11.

(a) The condition b<c+db<c+d is not a restriction on the parameters: in the complementary situation d<a+b,d<a+b, one has the factorization

(b) The identity (28) is an instance of a general result of [22] for beta-hypergeometric distributions. With the notation of the introduction in [22], one has indeed

∼\displaystyle\sim BH⁡(b,c+d−b,c+d,c,a+b+c)∼BH⁡(M​v)\displaystyle{\rm BH}(b,c+d-b,c+d,c,a+b+c)\;\sim\;{\rm BH}(Mv)

with v=(a,c,a+b−d,0,a+b),v=(a,c,a+b-d,0,a+b), whereas 𝐁a,c∼BH⁡(v){\bf B}_{a,c}\sim{\rm BH}(v) and 𝐁c+d−b,b′∼βΠ​v(2).{\bf B}^{\prime}_{c+d-b,b}\sim\beta^{(2)}_{\Pi v}. Therefore, (28) is a consequence of (5) in [22]. 5.5. The case of Mill’s ratio

The function r:ℝ↦(0,∞)r:{\mathbb{R}}\mapsto(0,\infty) defined by

r(x)=ex2/2∫x∞e−t2/2dtr(x)\;=\;e^{x^{2}/2}\int_{x}^{\infty}e^{-t^{2}/2}dt

is known in the literature as Mill’s ratio of the Gaussian law, whereas its reciprocal 1/r⁡(x)1/r(x) is called the Gaussian hazard rate. This function, which appears countlessly in the literature, is related to the case a=b=1/2a=b=1/2 of the present paper by the representations

r⁡(2​x)=2​H−1​(x)=π2​𝔼​[e−2​x​𝚪1/2],x∈ℝr(\sqrt{2}\,x)\;=\;\sqrt{2}\,H_{-1}(x)\;=\;\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}}\,{\mathbb{E}}\left[e^{-2x\sqrt{{\bf\Gamma}_{1/2}}}\right],\qquad x\in{\mathbb{R}} (29)

and

r⁡(2​x)=12​Ψ​(1/2,1/2,x)=π2​𝔼​[e−x​𝐁1/2,1/2′],x≥0.r(\sqrt{2x})\;=\;\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\,\Psi(1/2,1/2,x)\;=\;\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}}\,{\mathbb{E}}\left[e^{-x{\bf B}^{\prime}_{1/2,1/2}}\right],\qquad x\geq 0. (30)

The second equality in (29) implies that x↦r⁡(x)x\mapsto r(x) is LCM on (0,∞)(0,\infty) by Corollary 4, and that it is up to normalization the MGF of the r.v. −2​𝚪1/2,-2\sqrt{{\bf\Gamma}_{1/2}}, so that x↦r⁡(x)x\mapsto r(x) is also log-convex on ℝ.{\mathbb{R}}. The second equality in (30) entails that x↦r⁡(x)x\mapsto r(\sqrt{x}) is HCM on (0,∞)(0,\infty) as the Laplace transform of a generalized Gamma convolution - see Theorem 5.4.1. in [8], and by Property v) p.68 in [8] that the function x↦r⁡(ex)x\mapsto r(e^{x}) is log-concave on ℝ,{\mathbb{R}}, or equivalently that the function x↦x​r′​(x)/r⁡(x)x\mapsto xr^{\prime}(x)/r(x) is non-increasing on (0,∞).(0,\infty). The above discussion gives hence a short proof of parts (a) and (b) of Theorem 2.5 in [4]. Here is a simple improvement of parts (c) and (d) of this theorem.

Proposition 9.

One has the following monotonicity properties.

(a) On (0,∞),(0,\infty), the function x↦xα​r​(x)x\mapsto x^{\alpha}r(x) is decreasing for α=0,\alpha=0, increasing for α=1\alpha=1, and increasing then decreasing for α∈(0,1).\alpha\in(0,1).

(b) On (0,∞),(0,\infty), the function x↦xα​r′​(x)x\mapsto x^{\alpha}r^{\prime}(x) is increasing for α=0,\alpha=0, decreasing for α=2\alpha=2, and decreasing then increasing for α∈(0,2).\alpha\in(0,2).

Proof.

Changing the variable, we need for (a) to show the property for the function x↦eα​x​r​(ex)x\mapsto e^{\alpha x}r(e^{x}) on ℝ.{\mathbb{R}}. Observe from the preceding discussion that this function is log-concave and hence unimodal. Therefore, we need to evaluate the limits at ±∞\pm\infty, which are clearly both zero for α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1), zero and one for α=1\alpha=1 and π/2\sqrt{\pi/2} and zero for α=0.\alpha=0. This completes the proof of (a). The argument for (b) is the same, starting from the fact that

−r′​(2​x)=−x​Ψx′​(1/2,1/2,x)=xπ​∫0∞e−x​t​t1+t​𝑑t-r^{\prime}(\sqrt{2x})\;=\;-\sqrt{x}\,\Psi^{\prime}_{x}(1/2,1/2,x)\;=\;\sqrt{\frac{x}{\pi}}\,\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-xt}\,\frac{\sqrt{t}}{1+t}\;dt

is also HCM by Property iv) p.68, Theorem 5.4.1, Theorem 4.3.1 and Section 3.5 in [8], since the function t↦e−ε​t​t/(1+t)t\mapsto e^{-\varepsilon t}\sqrt{t}/(1+t) is up to normalization an HCM density for every ε>0.\varepsilon>0. Hence, the function x↦−eα​x​r′​(ex)x\mapsto-e^{\alpha x}r^{\prime}(e^{x}) is log-concave and unimodal on ℝ{\mathbb{R}} for every α∈ℝ,\alpha\in{\mathbb{R}}, and we can apply the same argument as above.

□\square

Let us now state, as a consequence of Theorem A, a series of CM properties for Mill’s ratio and its derivatives, which were actually the starting point of this paper.

For every integer n,n, the function

It is clear from (13) that Hν′=−2​ν​H−ν−1H_{\nu}^{\prime}=-2\nu H_{-\nu-1} and, combining this with the first equality in (29), we get

As a by-product of Corollary 9, let us also mention a new proof of an old and accurate upper bound on Mill’s ratio due to Sampford [24]. Other proofs of this classic inequality can be found e.g. in Proposition 3 of [29] or in Theorem 2.3 of [4], and we do not claim that our argument is comparatively simple.

The convexity of x↦1/r⁡(x)x\mapsto 1/r(x) on ℝ+{\mathbb{R}}^{+} is also a consequence of the case n=0n=0 in Proposition 10.

We next state the following open problem on Mill’s ratio and its derivatives, which is a refinement of Proposition 10. Recall indeed that if a function ff is CM, then so is x↦f⁡(x).x\mapsto f(\sqrt{x}). The statements are supported by simulations, but we could not find any proof.

For every integer n,n, the function

z↦−(r(n)​(z))2r(2​n+1)​(z)z\;\mapsto\;-\frac{\left(r^{(n)}(z)\right)^{2}}{r^{(2n+1)}(z)}

𝔼⁡[(𝚪a+𝚪a)s]\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}\left[\left(\!\sqrt{{\bf\Gamma}_{a}}+\sqrt{{\bf\Gamma}_{a}}\right)^{s}\right] =\displaystyle= 42−2​a(Γ⁡(a))2​∫0∞∫01us+4​a−1​e−u2​(21+z2)2​a+s/2​(1−z2)2​a−1​𝑑u​𝑑z\displaystyle\frac{4^{2-2a}}{({\Gamma}(a))^{2}}\int_{0}^{\infty}\!\!\int_{0}^{1}u^{s+4a-1}e^{-u^{2}}\left(\frac{2}{1+z^{2}}\right)^{2a+s/2}\!\!(1-z^{2})^{2a-1}\,du\,dz
=\displaystyle= Γ⁡(2​a+s/2)Γ⁡(2​a)×(41−2​a​Γ​(2​a)(Γ⁡(a))2​∫01(21+z2)2​a+s/2​(1−z2)2​a−1​𝑑z)\displaystyle\frac{{\Gamma}(2a+s/2)}{{\Gamma}(2a)}\,\times\,\left(\frac{4^{1-2a}\,{\Gamma}(2a)}{({\Gamma}(a))^{2}}\int_{0}^{1}\left(\frac{2}{1+z^{2}}\right)^{2a+s/2}\!\!(1-z^{2})^{2a-1}\,dz\right)
=\displaystyle= 𝔼[(𝚪2​a)s]×(21−4​a​Γ​(2​a)(Γ⁡(a))2∫01(21+z)2​a+s/2(1−z)2​a−1z−1/2dz)\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}\left[\left(\sqrt{{\bf\Gamma}_{2a}}\right)^{\!s}\right]\times\,\left(\frac{2^{1-4a}\,{\Gamma}(2a)}{({\Gamma}(a))^{2}}\int_{0}^{1}\left(\frac{2}{1+z}\right)^{2a+s/2}\!\!(1-z)^{2a-1}\,z^{-1/2}\,dz\right)
=\displaystyle= 𝔼⁡[(𝚪2​a)s]×𝔼⁡[((21+𝐁1/2,2​a)(2​a))s]\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}\left[\left(\sqrt{{\bf\Gamma}_{2a}}\right)^{\!s}\right]\times\,{\mathbb{E}}\left[\left(\sqrt{\left(\frac{2}{1+{\bf B}_{1/2,2a}}\right)^{(2a)}}\right)^{\!\!s\,}\right]

for every s>−4​a.s>-4a. Identifying the Mellin factors, we are reduced to show the identity

(21+𝐁1/2,2​a)(2​a)=d  1+𝐁a,1/2,\left(\frac{2}{1+{\bf B}_{1/2,2a}}\right)^{(2a)}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\;\,1\;+\;\sqrt{{\bf B}_{a,1/2}}\,,

which follows from the fact that the density of the random variable on both sides is proportional to (x−1)2​a−1(2x−x2)−1/2(x-1)^{2a-1}(2x-x^{2})^{-1/2} on (1,2).(1,2). We omit details.

□\square

We would like to conclude the paper with the following curious identity, which is a direct consequence of (1), Theorem A and Proposition 11.

Corollary 12.

For every a>0,a>0, one has

𝐁′a,1/2+𝐁′a,1/2=d(𝚪a+𝚪a)2𝚪1/2⋅{\bf B}^{\prime}_{a,1/2}\,+\,{\bf B}^{\prime}_{a,1/2}\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\;\frac{\left(\sqrt{{\bf\Gamma}_{a}}+\sqrt{{\bf\Gamma}_{a}}\right)^{2}}{{\bf\Gamma}_{1/2}}\cdot
